cognate: Ved. urú- = Gk εὐρύς (*h₁wérHu- 'wide'); Ved. pánthā-/path- = Gk πόντος (*pónteh₁- / *pont-h₁- 'path, passage').
drift_or_renewal: drift in Greek: *pont- 'way, passage' > πόντος 'open sea' (the sea conceived as the route one crosses; cf. Lat. pons, Arm. hun 'ford'); the adjective is unchanged.
shared_syntax: attributive adjective + noun in agreement, the NP being the route or place of a motion: loc. uraú pathí ~ dat.-loc. εὐρέι πόντῳ; acc. urúm ... pánthām ~ acc. (ἐπ') εὐρέα πόντον; instr. pathā́ urúṇā 'along the wide path'.
context: Vedic: the wide way along which gods stand or travel, the Soma-falcon flies, the chariot or the sun goes (RV 3.54.9, 4.26.5, 8.68.13, 1.24.8, 5.47.2, 10.107.1). Homeric: the wide sea as the route ships cross or on which one is held (ἐπιπλὼς εὐρέα πόντον Il. 6.291, ἐπ' εὐρέα πόντον ἄγουσι Il. 9.72, περήσαμεν εὐρέα πόντον Od. 24.118, κατερύκεται εὐρέι πόντῳ Od. 1.197), so the Greek keeps the travel frame that explains the drift. Both words are exact cognates in the same NP, recurrent in each tradition (≥6 Vedic, 9 Homeric lines), and the Greek collocation shows the old sense 'way' under the new sense 'sea'. 'Wide road' is a natural phrase, which is the main reason this stops short of certainty; the drift and the kept travel context argue against chance. Il. 2.145 (Εὖρος the wind) and RV 5.1.11c (urú goes with antárikṣam) in the same bundle are false hits.
phrase: *h₁wérHus pónteh₁s 'wide way' > Ved. urú- pánthā- ~ Gk εὐρὺς πόντος

cognate: Ved. √rej- 'tremble, quake' = Gk ἐλελίζω 'make quiver, shake' (*leyg-, also OE lācan); Ved. tvíṣ- 'violent agitation, vehemence' = Gk σείω 'shake' (*tweys-).
drift_or_renewal: renewal of the subject: Ved. dyaúḥ 'heaven' ~ Gk Ὄλυμπος (the gods' seat standing for heaven). Voice differs: Ved. intransitive rejata 'heaven trembled'; Il. 8.199 and 1.530 transitive 'made Olympus quake', HH 28.9 middle ἐλελίζετ’ 'Olympus quaked'.
shared_syntax: a *leyg- verb with sky/Olympus as the thing that trembles, in the same clause as, or next to, a *tweys- word for the god's agitation (tviṣáḥ ~ σείσατο / σείσασ’); in the next verse the earth trembles or cries out too (RV éjat bhū́miḥ; HH ἀμφὶ δὲ γαῖα ... ἰάχησεν).
context: Theophany at a god's birth or in a god's anger: RV 4.17.2 'at the birth of your vehemence heaven trembled, the earth shook for fear of your fury' (Indra; cf. RV 4.22.4 dyaúḥ ... jániman rejata kṣā́ḥ); HH 28.8-10 Athena springs from Zeus's head 'shaking her sharp spear, and great Olympus quaked ... the earth cried out'; Il. 8.198-9 Hera in anger 'shook herself on her throne and made tall Olympus quake'; Il. 1.530 Zeus's nod 'made great Olympus quake'. The match is two cognate roots together (*leyg- with the sky as what trembles, *tweys- for the god's motion), with birth as the setting in both RV 4.17 and HH 28. The world shaking at a god is a widespread motif, but this verb pairing is specific.
phrase: 'at the god's birth/wrath heaven (Olympus) trembles': Ved. tviṣáḥ jániman rejata dyaúḥ ~ Gk σείσασ’ ... ἐλελίζετ’ Ὄλυμπος

cognate: Ved. āmá- = Gk ὠμός 'raw' (*h₂eh₃mó-); Ved. pakvá- (√pac-) = Gk πέπων 'ripe/cooked' (*pekʷ-), Lat. coctus.
drift_or_renewal: Lat. renews 'raw' with crudus (crudum an coctum, Pl. Aul. 430); Hom. renews 'cooked' with ὀπταλέος (ὀπταλέα τε καὶ ὠμά Od. 12.396).
shared_syntax: polar pair in one clause, raw vs. cooked/ripe set side by side (Ved. āmā́(su) pakvám; Gk ὠμός ἢ πέπων, πέπονα ... μὴ ὠμά).
context: Vedic: the riddle of the cooked (milk) inside the raw (cow), a fixed formula (≥8 RV pādas). Greek: ripeness of fruit, humours or men (Ar. Eq. 260; Hippocratic). The contexts are not congruent and the antonymy is lexical, so this is at most an old polar pair carried by cognates in both branches, not a shown phrase.
